vignette:
Kofi was 22 and already carrying the weight of a role that many people assumed belonged to someone much older. As a school principal, he spent his days moving between classrooms, meeting with teachers, settling disputes in the hallway, and trying to stay composed in front of students who watched his every expression. He had a steady relationship with his girlfriend, who knew him as attentive and careful, yet he was increasingly aware that parts of his life no longer felt under his control. He had grown up in an African family in the United States, and when he first came to therapy it was not because he could point to one clear problem, but because he had become frightened by how often the past seemed to break into the present.

The experiences he now spoke about had their roots in childhood, when he lived with a caregiver who used physical punishment in a way Kofi experienced as frightening and humiliating rather than disciplinary. He did not describe the abuse in a smooth, continuous story. When asked to recall it deliberately, he found it difficult to access the memory at all, as though the events sat behind a locked door. What came instead were disconnected pieces: the sting of being grabbed by the arm, the sound of a voice rising, the look of a room becoming suddenly dangerous, the sensation of bracing himself before the next blow. He said those fragments did not fit together in his mind, and that was part of what distressed him; the memory felt more real and vivid than ordinary memories, yet also strangely incomplete, as if he could see flashes of it more clearly than experiences from last week.

As a child he learned to keep his body still and his emotions hidden, and as an adult he remained sensitive to situations that seemed unpredictable. In his work at the school, there were moments that unexpectedly pulled him back into that old state of alarm: a parent arriving unannounced and demanding to speak immediately, a student suddenly shouting in a corridor, or a staff meeting taking an abrupt turn that left him unsure what would happen next. He noticed that unpredictability itself could make his chest tighten and his attention sharpen, as if he were bracing for something he could not prepare for. Even at home, ordinary interruptions could leave him on edge if plans changed without warning. He did not describe these moments as flashbacks, but as sudden periods in which he felt emotionally caught off guard by a kind of danger he could not neatly name.

Old photographs were another potent trigger. He had tried, at first, to look through family pictures with his girlfriend, only to find that certain images-particularly those from childhood-brought on a wave of unease that made him want to put them away quickly. A photo of himself as a boy, posed in a school uniform, could leave him staring at the image with a kind of estrangement, struck by how real the past felt in that instant and how little of it he could confidently explain. At times, a nightmare would lead to the same feeling upon waking: he would jolt awake with the residue of the dream still clinging to him, momentarily unable to settle into the room around him. In those early minutes after waking, the line between what he had dreamed and what had happened years before could feel uncomfortably thin.

Over time, Kofi came to hold several painful beliefs about himself. He was frightened by the idea that he would not be able to control his anger and might do something terrible. He described this not as a sudden impulse to harm someone, but as a fear that anger itself lived too close to the surface and could spill out in a way he would regret. As a principal, that fear made him watch himself carefully during tense conversations, especially when students or adults challenged him. He also believed he had permanently changed for the worse. He spoke about this in a subdued, matter-of-fact way, as though some essential part of him had been altered and could not simply be restored. Alongside that, he felt a deep sense that he could not stop bad things from happening to him. In situations that were uncertain or difficult to predict, he often felt as if he were waiting for the next blow, even when nothing outwardly dangerous was occurring.

These experiences had begun to affect his daily life in concrete ways. He became more guarded in situations at school that involved sudden conflict, and he noticed himself withdrawing from moments that might expose him to unexpected emotions. His girlfriend had seen him go quiet after waking from a nightmare, and he struggled to explain why a simple photograph or an unplanned interruption could leave him feeling shaken. What finally brought him to seek help was the accumulating sense that he was living with a constant readiness for danger and with fear about his own temper. He wanted relief from the nightmares, from the unsettling force of old images, and from the conviction that something in him had been permanently damaged. More than anything, Kofi hoped that he could learn to trust his own reactions again and no longer feel that the past was waiting to break open in the middle of his present life.
